styles.executable_prompt_template:
Replace all double-brace placeholders with task inputs before execution. Use documented defaults only for omitted optional inputs and state the assumptions.
Create a Whiteboard Animation video about {{subject}} for {{audience_and_objective}}. Use {{assets_and_exact_copy}}. Deliver a video of {{duration_seconds}} seconds, with aspect ratio {{aspect_ratio}}, resolution {{resolution}}, and frame rate {{frame_rate}}. Follow {{audio_or_rhythm_requirements}} and save deliverables to {{output_directory}}.
Use {{render_pipeline}} for composition and export only. If omitted, resolve it to tech.framework_selection.default. Check the primary framework first; use tech.framework_selection.fallback only when the documented fallback_condition is met, and record the verified reason. An existing React project alone is not sufficient reason to switch.
1. Inspect the project, available tools, assets, exact wording, and input formats. Reuse suitable existing components. Treat visual_cues as art-direction constraints and choose only the tech.recommended_stack entries needed for the selected framework and asset-generation method. Example dimensions, palette sizes, beats, and scenes apply only when the task adopts them.
2. Write a short storyboard with explicit time ranges. Give each section one main idea, a clear focal point, and enough reading or observation time. Plan staging around this style's visual rules: Use a clean pale background, simplified line diagrams, and legible lettering. Draw only objects that help explain the subject. Reveal diagrams in causal order, then add annotations; use erasure or redrawing transitions with sufficient reading pauses. Add secondary styles only when their materials, composition, and movement remain compatible.
3. Implement the style-specific technique: Organize diagram paths and text layers in advance. Reveal them in explanatory order; do not invent a drawing hand when none is provided. Keep Canvas, DOM, and WebGL in the browser and file processing in Node.js or Python. Drive visual updates from shared, seekable video time; load fonts and assets, seed randomness, and cache stateful simulation. Centralize colors, fonts, dimensions, camera settings, and timing. Build representative frames and key actions before expanding the sequence.
4. Follow only the tech.render_pipeline route for {{render_pipeline}}. Distinguish drawing or pose-exposure rate from delivery frame rate. Use task-provided or authorized audio, and synchronize picture and sound against the same time data. Match composition and velocity at loop boundaries.
5. Render and inspect actual opening, key-action, transition, and closing frames, then watch the decoded video. Check the style-specific constraints in visual_cues, readable text, correct glyphs, stable materials and outlines, missing assets, crop margins, timing, dimensions, and audio synchronization. Fix issues and rerender until the relevant checks pass; compilation alone is insufficient.
6. Deliver the video, editable source or project, a key-frame contact sheet, chosen parameters, and reproducible render instructions. State any missing assets or unverified limitations. Distinguish photographed production from simulated appearance.
Framework contract: select the packages, runtime, timeline registration, validation commands, and renderer that actually belong to {{render_pipeline}}. Do not mix another framework's hooks, composition lifecycle, or renderer. Specialist modeling, photography, drawing, and scientific computation can produce inputs for the selected video framework without being replaced by it.
Palette contract: read palette before implementation. Use its suggested tokens only when task, brand, or reference colors are absent. Keep supplied exact colors, source artwork, existing semantic assignments, and style color-family and color-count constraints unchanged. Use chroma-js to validate and normalize equivalent color values, select readable existing foreground/background pairs, and interpolate only when palette.gradient is enabled. Do not recolor assets or add hues to improve contrast; change text placement, an existing backing color, or typography instead. Follow palette.agent_instruction and inspect actual composited frames.
Optional sketch rendering: when the brief calls for sketch-like marks, consult the Rough.js entry in tech.recommended_stack. Use package roughjs to generate seeded Canvas/SVG geometry, preserve the resolved palette, and follow its style_application and integration_guidance. Cache shapes; let the selected timeline animate transforms, masks, reveals or authored pose variants. Rough.js does not supply handwriting, authentic drawing media, a character rig or frame-by-frame poses. Keep precise text, measured geometry and approved source assets intact.
Shared movement quality: follow shared_motion_guidance and tech.motion_guidance. Design coherent trajectories, acceleration, transitions and settling with readable holds. Use time-based interpolation and authored easing when appropriate; preserve deliberate cuts, impacts, stepped exposure, whole-pixel placement and line-boil cadence. Do not automatically add springs, bounce, floating or extra in-between poses. Derive state from composition time; bake or deterministically replay any stateful smoothing, physics or camera damping. Verify direct, backward and out-of-order seeks plus the decoded sequence and loop seams. Keep the existing palette and style-specific motion direction intact.
Cytoscape.js option: For scenes containing meaningful node-edge relationships, optionally select Cytoscape.js from tech.recommended_stack. Compute relationship diagram structure and positions, then render authored SVG or Canvas strokes in explanatory drawing order; retain whiteboard typography and stroke treatment. Follow its graph validation, layout, algorithm and rendering guidance. Cache layouts and analysis, drive highlights and movement from composition time, and preserve exact graph meaning, palette tokens, style cadence and the selected framework render_pipeline. Use a custom visual renderer where required by the style.
Anime.js option: Optionally select Anime.js from tech.recommended_stack when its documented animation features help the scene. Reveal prepared SVG diagram strokes in explanatory order, retaining authored text and reading holds. Follow its integration_guidance, constraints and verification. Retain the selected framework render_pipeline and the HyperFrames GSAP master timeline contract; use Anime.js only through a verified time adapter with separate property ownership. Preserve palette tokens, exact copy, shared_motion_guidance and style cadence.
Paper.js option: Optionally select Paper.js from tech.recommended_stack when vector path geometry or Canvas rendering is useful. Prepare diagram paths and sample path length for deterministic drawing reveals; retain explanatory order and readable labels. Follow its suggested_methods, integration_guidance, constraints and verification. Evaluate geometry from fixed rest states at composition time, explicitly update the view, and preserve palette tokens, original contour character, style cadence and the selected framework render_pipeline.
Production ownership: follow production_policy. Choose the style_renderer and motion_engine from the style and motion requirements first, and state the selected tools and their responsibilities. Build the visuals and movement with those tools according to tech.implementation and visual_cues. Use {{render_pipeline}} only for scene assembly, seekable composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and export. Keep specialist rendering and motion logic in their own layers; do not substitute generic framework text, DOM transitions, or framework animation helpers merely because the pipeline is available. Native DOM or SVG is appropriate when it actually satisfies the style. Integrate deterministic time-driven layers or baked assets, and verify representative visuals and motion before assembling the full video.
Audio direction: follow audio_direction. Based on {{subject}}, {{audience_and_objective}}, the storyboard, visual_cues, and motion direction, suggest suitable background music, voiceover, sung vocals, sound effects, ambience, or silence. Honor {{audio_or_rhythm_requirements}} first. State the proposed choices and why they fit this topic and style; suggest mood, texture, energy, tempo where useful, voice language and delivery where useful, and scene-level audio changes. Do not impose a fixed soundtrack rule or include every layer. Source or create authorized assets, then use {{render_pipeline}} for assembly, synchronization, mixing, and export. Verify speech intelligibility, audio balance, absence of clipping, and picture synchronization in the final video.

sources.style_evidence: Contour-only robot and bicycle with limited internal detail, uniform stroke widths and connected joints on a plain field.
sources.palette_lesson: These frames use a monochrome palette: black strokes and type on a flat near-white field, gray for secondary labels and code comments, and no hue accents. Hierarchy comes from stroke weight, bold vs regular monospace and gray value. The near-white canvas is this author's example, not a rule. What defines the style is a single flat, untextured field with one high-contrast line color and at most one value step for secondary text. For new subjects the field can follow the scene, provided the line color is inverted or adjusted to keep strong contrast. Options: a deep charcoal or ink-navy field with off-white lines for a night or technical topic; pale cool gray-blue for infrastructure or data; soft sage or mint-gray for health or nature; slate with pale lines for security; a muted terracotta or dusty rose field with dark lines for a warmer consumer story. If an accent is used, give it one semantic job (cursor, active state, a single highlight), keep it scarce, and recheck caption and code contrast against the new field.

sources.style_evidence: The line-weight hierarchy runs from heavy object contours to hairline graticule to outline-only watermark type. Diagonal hatching gives limited internal detail, and a single crimson accent marks emphasis.
sources.palette_lesson: The fixed part of this style is the system: one dark ink tone for all structure and type, a lighter tint of the same ink for the graticule and watermark, and one saturated accent kept for data markers and captions. The background is a mottled, vignetted surface whose texture reads as a physical substrate. The warm tan aged-paper colour is this author's example, chosen to suit an 'origins of money' history theme. It is not a required canvas. The sampled composite values are uniformly warm light tan, but those include the ink. Keep the accent's job (it marks progress dots and category captions) and keep it rare. Recheck contrast so the hairline graticule stays faint but visible and the small sans labels remain readable on whatever ground you choose.

Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

sources.palette_lesson: The mint-gray to near-white gradient with mint and teal bokeh dots is this author's choice of mood: calm and clinical-gentle, which suits a healthcare and patient-communication topic. It is not a requirement of the style. What defines the style is the set of roles: (1) a low-contrast, quiet, tinted field; (2) opaque white pills and bubbles as the reading surface, so text contrast stays independent of the background; (3) one dark ink color for all type and line art; (4) one accent hue family reused in the decorative dots and the character details. To adapt it, keep the white-card plus dark-ink reading layer and choose a new field and accent pair for each subject. Examples: dusty lavender to white with lilac dots for sleep or wellness; pale peach to warm white with coral dots for food or family; soft sky-blue to white with aqua dots for travel or weather; muted sage with olive dots for gardening; a deep slate-navy field with white cards and soft amber dots for an evening or night topic. Recheck that the dots never sit at high contrast behind card edges. Sampled exact source hex values are not claimed. sources.style_evidence: The fish, pickups, buttons and chevrons are clean flat vector fills with consistent rounded forms and no outline or shading. A small fixed set of cyan, magenta, white and gold carries through every frame.

Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. sources.style_evidence: A recognizable character in a narrative meadow environment with small props (flowers, mushrooms, vines), warm character colors, an overall grain texture, drawn outlines, and expression changes across seconds 1, 3, 5 and 8.
sources.palette_lesson: The fixed part of this example is a lighting-driven palette system laid over one unchanging landscape layout: the same mountains, lake, meadow, flowers and foliage are recolored for dusk (violet-to-peach), day (clear blue with an orange sun), cosmic night (indigo-violet nebula) and moonlit night (navy and slate). The character keeps a single warm terracotta local color throughout, so it is always the warmest and most saturated mass and stays the focal point against every sky. Glow effects (rings, HUD panels, fireflies, mushrooms) use pale cyan, white or yellow-green additive light and stay small. The specific sky hues, the planet and moon, and the terracotta mascot color are this author's choices for this subject, not style requirements. What carries over is one consistent local color for the hero, a sky/time-of-day gradient that sets the mood, and environment colors that shift together as a single lighting state.

Once inside the world (7–8s), the background follows the scene: a striped dusk sky in dusty blue, rose, salmon and pale yellow over sage-green hills. For new subjects, choose the sky and ground to fit the setting and time of day. Keep values soft and close together, with darker outlines and small saturated accents (sun, flowers, a character's clothing) as focal points. Recheck contrast so figures stay readable against the banded backgrounds.

Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

sources.style_evidence: Black-bordered panel with drop shadow, caption boxes, title banner, an issue tag and a 'KA-POW!' SFX starburst at the reveal moment (6–8s).
sources.palette_lesson: Only 5–8s carry style evidence; 1–4s are dark app/browser screen recording. The yellow side fill is pillarbox surround, not the comic canvas. The author's own choices are the lemon-yellow surround, the orange sunburst with orange-red dots and a teal inner image, which complements the warm frame. What the medium actually requires is a limited set of saturated print-ink families, black keylines and drop shadows, a halftone dot texture with a fixed grid, light caption/tag boxes, and SFX colors chosen to contrast with whatever image sits under them. The sunburst and border should take their hue from the subject and mood, and the inner image should be complementary or contrasting so the panel reads clearly.

sources.style_evidence: At s8, radial concentration or speed lines and an impact stamp land as a comic-style emphasis beat over a screentone ground.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's example is fully achromatic: a mid-charcoal halftone ground, black-ink objects with white keylines, off-white paper cards and white LED dots. A darker near-black overlay is used for the spotlight beat. The measured composite dominant shifts from mid grey (s1–6) to very dark grey (s7–8). That reflects the dimming overlay, not a second palette. What defines the style is not grey itself. It is the print constraint: tone made by dot density in one ink against a substrate, plus solid ink badges and stamps, with emphasis carried by luminance and inversion rather than hue. For new subjects the ground can be any single ink-on-substrate pairing that suits the scene. Keep paper cards (or the subject's equivalent) as the brightest plane. Reserve the darkest overlay for focus moments, and check that the small text on cards stays legible over the dot screen. If one accent is added, it should be a spot-ink color with a fixed semantic role (e.g., 'hit' state), not decoration.

styles.visual_cues: Authored manga illustration with subject-specific storytelling: people, animals, creatures, monsters, objects, machines, environments or abstract subjects as required by the brief. Use controlled ink line weights, selective screentones, cinematic panel composition and purposeful negative space. Choose establishing views and expressive or structural close-ups that reveal the actual subject; human faces, eyes and hands are optional, never a required template. Drawing quality must carry a still frame; generic icons, dashboard cards or a blanket dot filter are not substitutes for refined manga drawing.

tech.implementation: Subject selection: Manga is a visual storytelling language, not a requirement for human characters. Let the brief choose people, animals, creatures, monsters, objects, machines, environments or abstract subjects; do not default to a person, human face, eye close-up or hand insert. Do not anthropomorphize objects unless the story calls for it. For animals use species-specific proportions, stance, joints, gait and surface forms; for monsters establish coherent invented anatomy and repeatable features; for objects and machines use perspective, structural joins, material response, function and mechanical articulation; for environments use spatial depth, scale, architecture or natural forms; for abstract subjects establish consistent visual rules and meaningful transformations. Apply convincing volume, clear silhouette, intentional line-weight hierarchy, purposeful ink masses, contact and perspective to every subject. Select panels and details for this story, never a mandatory portrait/eye/hand montage. Human anatomy, eyes, hands, hair and clothing examples below are conditional techniques only when the selected subject actually has those features; they never require adding a human or human features. Separate subject line art, form/material layers, environmental perspective, shadow masks, screentones, panel borders and lettering. Include hair/clothing shapes only when present. Study the reference at full resolution before building: identify contour weights, proportions, hand anatomy, hair clumps, cloth folds, spatial perspective, tone placement and panel-to-panel continuity. Use original characters and settings; do not copy reference characters, dialogue, watermarks or branding. At 1280px width use roughly 3–5px silhouette emphasis, 1–2px structural contours and 0.5–1px fine detail, scaled with delivery size; use tapered filled strokes for eyelashes and select contour accents, with clean joins instead of uniform icon outlines. Construct convincing subject volume, functional structure and contact. For subjects with those features, construct face volumes and eye placement, hands with readable gesture and joints, hair with grouped strands and directional highlights, and fabric folds rooted in tension or contact. Reserve solid ink for occlusion, deep shadows and focal accents. Clip a small number of stable screentone densities and directional hatching to form and shadow planes; retain quiet white highlights and gutters instead of dotting every surface. Keep screen-tone spacing stable during masking, scaling, and pose changes, and inspect moire at actual delivery resolution. Establish foreground/midground/background and consistent perspective; do not let construction lines show through opaque objects. Choose asymmetric panels according to narrative function, selecting wider settings, relevant structural/material details or expressive close-ups without forcing a portrait/eye/hand sequence or any repeated template. Let panels appear in deliberate reading order and hold long enough to understand; use subject-appropriate action only when supported by the beat: weight transfer, animal movement, mechanical articulation, material deformation, motivated camera motion, or blink/breath/hand action when those features exist. Avoid perpetual wobble, indiscriminate speed lines, bouncing panels or changing character identity between shots. Derive all pose and panel states from seekable composition time. Finish a representative still before adding motion: inspect silhouette at thumbnail size, anatomy and line joins at full resolution, tone clipping, gutter consistency, lettering fit and subject continuity. Do not substitute a simple eye symbol, abstract nodes or triangles for an illustrated story. Code-only drawing contract: Author every story illustration directly in editable SVG paths or deterministic Canvas drawing code, including faces, hair, hands, clothing, environments, screentones and panel masks. Do not substitute AI-generated images, raster artwork, image sprites, traced generated artwork or a finished illustration with reveal overlays. Improve the code-drawn shapes themselves: use authored Bezier contours, tapered filled strokes, grouped strand shapes, intentional shadow planes and selective procedural hatching. Simplify anatomy deliberately to a coherent graphic manga vocabulary when necessary; do not promise generated-image detail that the code cannot reproduce. Animation must control the authored drawing layers and derive all states from time. Use actual subject/story artwork; do not turn this style into a backstage director-and-crew viewer. Respect approved palette and assets; a reference accent color is not permission to expand the selected palette. SVG refinement workflow: Block subject volume, silhouette, pose or structural arrangement, contact and perspective first; face landmarks and hand gesture apply only when relevant; then refine organic contours with cubic C/S Bezier paths and aligned tangent directions at smooth joins, reserving cusp corners for intentional points and creases. Improve control handles before adding more nodes. Express pressure-like ink accents as closed tapered filled shapes, not uniformly thick strokes. When the subject has eyes, build the eye from appropriate lid, lash, iris, pupil and highlight layers and reuse consistent proportions in close-ups. For a subject with hair or hands, group hair clumps around the skull with curved strand flow and reserved highlight shapes; construct fingers as overlapping curved volumes with joints, not an angular mitten. Give opaque subject shapes real base fills before adding clipped screentones and directional hatching. Keep secondary contours and texture subordinate to silhouette and focal ink masses. Inspect and revise the unanimated SVG at thumbnail and full output sizes before layering motion. Detailed paths must serve anatomy and form; increasing path count or blanket texture is not quality. Keep character, eye, hand, clothing, tone, panel and lettering layers individually editable and deterministically seekable. Artist-construction pass: Establish subject axes, mass balance, articulation, support and contact in a temporary construction view before final contours; head axis, shoulder gesture and palm/pen contact apply only to a figure doing that action. Choose one light direction; make shadow-side crevices and foreground overlaps heavier, and allow thinner or broken contours on lit edges instead of uniformly outlining every form. When hair is present, build hair as skull volume, root flow, large overlapping clumps, smaller strands and light-consistent highlights; avoid a rigid helmet with evenly spaced white slots. If a hand uses a pen, construct a pen grip from wrist angle, palm volume, thumb mass and finger gestures, checking actual contact and occlusion. Review the still with tone hidden, in an ink-only view, at full size, at thumbnail size and temporarily mirrored; correct eye alignment, jaw shape, silhouette and accidental tangencies before adding texture. Tone must follow surface and light, not decorate every region. Assess anatomy, expression and focal hierarchy by inspecting the rendered still; valid XML, extra paths, a longer SVG budget and passing technical tests do not prove drawing quality. Only then add deterministic movement. These construction and inking rules apply to any subject in this style; do not impose the sample character or composition. Character-quality construction (only for a subject with relevant head/face/body features, never a requirement to add them): Choose head yaw, pitch, tilt, gaze and emotion before final paths. Block skull volume, jaw planes, face centreline and a curved feature line; a 2D rotation is not a three-quarter head turn. Place eyes, brows, nose, mouth and ears on those forms using proportions appropriate to the intended character. A far eye must be angle-aware, narrower and nearer the nose where perspective requires; do not mirror identical front-facing eye symbols to represent a turned head. Keep eyelids wrapped around eye volume, with gaze shared by both eyes. Coordinate lid opening, brows and mouth to communicate the intended emotion rather than adding highlights for decoration. Establish a line of action and shoulder/torso relationship, and connect the neck to jaw and shoulders plausibly; avoid a static frontal mannequin when the story needs character acting. Build hair volume over the skull with overlapping clumps and root direction, not a black helmet hiding weak construction. Review an ink-only character with tone and highlights hidden: pose, head angle, gaze, expression, silhouette, near/far feature placement and hand-to-prop contact must read before detail. Compare full-size, thumbnail and mirrored views; correct structure before adding texture. Reuse design proportions across shots while authoring angle-specific contours. Maintain code-only editable drawing and derive movement from deterministic time. Eye-integrity pass (only when the chosen subject has visible eyes): Construct the pair on one head-volume and feature-line model with one shared gaze target; project each eye and iris for that view rather than independently nudging pupils by arbitrary pixels. Perspective can narrow the far eye without accidentally changing its lid opening or expression into a squint. Author the eye opening, sclera, lid contour and its clip path from matching landmarks in the same local coordinate space; changing an opening requires changing its mask and lid together. Keep iris and pupil clipped inside the eye opening, nest highlights inside the iris, and draw upper lids/occluding features above them. Check the visible iris against both lids at neutral and extreme gaze positions; avoid detached pupils, inconsistent occlusion and collapsed dark blobs. At preview-card scale simplify iris texture and catchlights before enlarging or distorting anatomy; fine screentone and multiple tiny highlights are optional. During gaze motion move the iris/pupil/highlight assembly together inside the lid mask; during a blink change the opening/occlusion coherently rather than scaling a complete eye symbol. Before animation, inspect an eye-pair crop and the whole head in a neutral pose at full size and actual card size. Then inspect gaze extremes, blink keyframes and the settled expression, including direct/backward seeks. Fix perspective, shared gaze, expression, clipping and small-scale readability before publishing; valid SVG or general render checks alone do not pass this eye review. Do not add eyes to subjects that do not need them.

Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider bounded pupil following with optional delayed brows, slight head tilt, and scheduled blinks. Require suitable facial layers or a rig, preserve expression and drawing cadence, and do not interpret this as viewer eye tracking.

Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Consider meaningful narrative steps with synchronized copy and visual states, plus optional within-step progress or sticky graphics. Use only scene-level motions that serve the story, and schedule the same states by time for video.

Use a cinematic opening with separately animated illustrated objects, speed-line accents and expressive motion text. Stage the action across panels and end in the approved composition. Prefer this over pupil-only movement or tiny ambient wiggles.

Limited-color lettering can replace phrases with reading holds and controlled glyph poses. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

A monochrome punctuation crop can connect authored panels without screen-tone distortion. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

sources.style_evidence: Rubber-hose character design: the bug minions have tube-like curving limbs, and the boss moon has bold, expressive cartoon features in the style of a 1930s cartoon.
sources.palette_lesson: The red-brown sepia monochrome here is this author's grading choice for a 'cursed vintage film / moon level' scene, not a requirement of the style. Measured composite dominance is only a near-black dark red, and it includes the curtains. The medium constraints that matter are structural. (1) Use one tinted tonal ramp: a dark ground, mid forms and pale highlights for effects, puffs and interactive items. (2) Reserve one saturated accent for the threat or focal point, here the red eyes, plus a tiny secondary accent such as the magenta target. (3) Let beams and light be translucent lighter values of the same family that let the hatching show through, not new hues. For new subjects, keep the single-ramp-plus-one-accent logic and choose the tint from the scene. For example: cold blue-gray moonlit monochrome for a night ocean, olive-green sepia for a swamp or jungle stage, a teal-cyan ramp with an orange accent for an underwater level, smoky violet for a haunted carnival, faded mustard-ochre for a desert daytime set, or a neutral silver-gray film look with a single red accent. Recheck that the accent and the HUD stay readable against whichever dark or light ground you pick.

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

sources.style_evidence: 3D environment with soft, controlled colour masses, painterly cloud shapes, stylized grass and rounded tree canopies. There are no glossy photoreal highlights, and the surfaces read as handled colour rather than PBR realism.
sources.palette_lesson: Colour here is a lighting and biome choice, not a fixed recipe. This example uses a midday temperate meadow: a soft, desaturated blue sky, white volumetric-looking clouds, a dominant saturated yellow-green field, and two small accent families (lavender-violet and ochre/rust) scattered as clusters. A neutral man-made focal object uses charcoal, off-white and warm timber. The transferable rules: one dominant ground colour field, one atmospheric sky gradient, and two or three sparse complementary accents placed in clusters near the camera. The focal object stays neutral, plus one warm accent so it reads. Keep values soft and contrast moderate. Haze should lighten and desaturate distance. The blue sky and green grass are this author's scene choices, not part of the style. The same craft works at dusk, in a dry summer or in snow by swapping the ground and sky families while keeping the accent-cluster logic.

sources.style_evidence: Stylized 3D environment with soft, painterly color masses in grass and sky, warm stylized lighting, haze and god-rays, and no glossy photoreal highlights. Grass blades act like directional painted strokes on the forms.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors seen here belong to this author's chosen scene. Golden-hour peach-amber haze, yellow-green and ochre grass, olive hills, chestnut and honey animals, and a teal plus red-brown costume accent describe one windswept-plain setting at one time of day. They are not rules of the style. What defines the style is the treatment: a 3D scene shaded as soft color masses, with atmospheric perspective that fades distant layers toward the sky color, one warm or cool key light, and saturation held at a moderate level. The UI belongs to a separate flat layer of light cream cards with dark text and one accent hue. For a new subject, build the palette from that subject's own environment and time of day. Then keep three roles: a hazy sky and depth gradient, a dominant ground-cover mass, and a small complementary accent on the hero subject. Recheck caption contrast against whatever the sky or ground becomes.

sources.style_evidence: Directional swirling brushwork in the sky, a flame-shaped cypress, rhythmic paint dabs, and a strong contrast between deep blue and yellow. The video explicitly uses one specific painting as its reference rather than generic swirls.
sources.palette_lesson: The deep ultramarine and cobalt, cyan-white and gold-yellow scheme belongs to this author's chosen reference painting (a night scene), not to the style itself. What defines the style is the medium logic: a dominant cool or warm field built from many directional brush dabs rather than flat colour; a small set of high-value complementary accents (here yellow halos and warm windows against blue) that act as light sources; and dark, saturated forms (the cypress) that anchor the composition. The near-black gallery wall and gilt frame are a presentation device around the canvas, not the canvas colour. The interface borrows the painting's blue and gold so it stays subordinate. Inside the 3D world the palette shifts with distance, from deep blue-green to lighter grey-green up close. The single most saturated warm accent, the orange cat, is reserved for the object the viewer should find. For a new subject, pick the field from that subject's light — daytime, dusk or interior — and keep one complementary accent family for focal points.

sources.style_evidence: The hill and sun use translucent mottled washes that pool darker in places, over visible paper grain. The bird has a wet pink-to-yellow blend.
sources.palette_lesson: These frames show one example palette, not a fixed recipe. The warm cream paper, sage-green hill, yellow sun and rose accent suit the creator's sunny 'sketchbook day' subject. The style itself is defined by medium rules: a visible textured paper substrate; black ink contours carrying the main value contrast and the lettering; a few translucent washes, each confined to its owning shape, with paper grain showing through and slight pooling; and large unpainted negative space, so the paper itself serves as the sky. For new subjects, keep those rules and let the scene choose the paper tone and wash hues. Possible directions: cool blue-grey paper with indigo and teal washes for night or rain; pale grey-green paper with moss and rust for a forest; a dusty pink paper ground with plum and orange for dusk; or bright white paper with cobalt and coral for a crisp, clean look. Keep ink dark enough to contrast with whatever paper tone you choose, and keep washes lighter in value than the ink. Use one or two saturated accents per scene; here, yellow and rose do that job.

styles.visual_cues: Use pressure-sensitive brush marks, diluted ink washes, deliberate empty space, and restrained tonal contrast. Choose a specific ink-painting tradition and preserve its compositional logic. Reveal strokes and washes coherently rather than using generic splashes or treating Chinese ink painting and Japanese sumi-e as interchangeable.
styles.note: A supplemental design reference; not claimed as a directly named style in the source collection. Chinese ink wash and Japanese sumi-e are related but distinct traditions.

tech.implementation: Use authentic ink assets or controlled brush and wash masks. Keep stroke direction, pigment layering, and negative space consistent.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.

Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. sources.style_evidence: Monochrome black ink on paper: a single brush stroke draws the ridge, stippled ink fills the peaks, and diluted pale ranges plus fog show distance, with large empty space. Composition follows Chinese shan-shui layered recession.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors that define the style come from the medium: carbon-black ink thinned into a ladder of greys, with a faint cool blue-grey cast in the most distant, most diluted layers. The paper is a pale substrate that shows through as fog and empty space. The warm off-white paper tone in this clip is the author's example for an autumn moon-night mood, not a requirement. Keep the ink value ladder (dense black foreground, mid-grey mid-ground, pale tinted distance, unpainted paper as mist) and choose the substrate per scene: cool grey-white xuan paper for winter or dawn, pale silk-celadon for spring water scenes, aged tea-brown silk for historical subjects, or a deep indigo-dyed or dusk-blue field with lighter pigment for night (inverting the value logic carefully). One restrained accent such as a vermilion seal or a pale moon wash is optional. Check that text keeps contrast against both the paper and the fog layers.

sources.style_evidence: Each character is preceded and surrounded by a diluted grey ink bloom that diffuses over time, together with pressure-like stroke ends and a large amount of deliberate empty paper. The ink treatment is closest to sumi-e, though there is no landscape imagery.
sources.palette_lesson: This is a monochrome ink-on-paper scene. Black ink is the only solid pigment, diluted grey washes add tone, and the ground is a pale warm-grey paper with fibres and a soft vignette. Mid-grey type is used for captions, and a thin grey line is the secondary graphic. The pale warm-grey paper colour is this author's example, not the definition of the style. What defines the style is the medium: one dense ink plus its own dilutions, a visibly fibrous paper ground, and the halo being the same ink diluted rather than a shadow or a new hue. No seal colour or other chroma appears in seconds 1–8. For new subjects, the paper can be cool grey, blue-grey, pale celadon, unbleached kraft or a dark charcoal sheet. On a dark sheet, invert to pale ink or gofun white and keep tonal dilution as the second value. An optional single restrained accent, such as a vermilion seal, should only be added if the subject justifies it. Recheck caption contrast after any change, because the low-contrast grey captions are already near the readability limit.

sources.style_evidence: Every frame's terrain is built from opaque, palette-knife oil/gouache-like slabs and thick white impasto foam with relief shading. The on-screen label 'OIL ON CANVAS' is author framing, not evidence; the visible brushwork alone supports this match.
sources.palette_lesson: Here the colours come from the subject: a beach at low tide gives turquoise/cyan sea, white foam and warm sand-ochre ground, with small saturated sprite accents (red/white umbrellas, purple pearls, green props) and cream plus golden-yellow caption type. Those hues are this author's choice for a beach, not rules of the style. The style constraints are different: (1) opaque paint covers the whole frame with no blank canvas showing; (2) each terrain zone gets a limited family of 2–3 close values built from overlapping knife slabs; (3) the brightest impasto (here the white foam) carries the relief highlights; (4) game sprites use small, saturated, high-chroma accents so they read against broad painted masses; (5) UI type is cream or white with dark outlines so it stays legible over any paint. For a new subject, take the terrain families from that environment and re-check caption contrast against the busiest area.

sources.style_evidence: Thick, visible oil-like strokes and impasto-style dabs on the canvas at 1–5 s. A gilt frame presents the image as a framed oil painting.
sources.palette_lesson: The deep ultramarine and cobalt, cyan-white and gold-yellow scheme belongs to this author's chosen reference painting (a night scene), not to the style itself. What defines the style is the medium logic: a dominant cool or warm field built from many directional brush dabs rather than flat colour; a small set of high-value complementary accents (here yellow halos and warm windows against blue) that act as light sources; and dark, saturated forms (the cypress) that anchor the composition. The near-black gallery wall and gilt frame are a presentation device around the canvas, not the canvas colour. The interface borrows the painting's blue and gold so it stays subordinate. Inside the 3D world the palette shifts with distance, from deep blue-green to lighter grey-green up close. The single most saturated warm accent, the orange cat, is reserved for the object the viewer should find. For a new subject, pick the field from that subject's light — daytime, dusk or interior — and keep one complementary accent family for focal points.

styles.visual_cues: Choose charcoal or pastel as the primary medium. Charcoal emphasizes tonal mass, hatching, and smudging; pastel allows softly layered pigment with visible grain. Preserve paper texture and localized powder edges while revealing or erasing marks; avoid uniform noise that obscures structure.
styles.note: A supplemental design reference; not claimed as a directly named style in the source collection. Charcoal and pastel are separate dry-media techniques.

tech.implementation: Use fixed grain brushes, smudge masks, and paper layers. Build charcoal values or pastel color layers separately and reveal marks locally.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. sources.palette_lesson: This is a monochrome ink-on-paper scene. Black ink is the only solid pigment, diluted grey washes add tone, and the ground is a pale warm-grey paper with fibres and a soft vignette. Mid-grey type is used for captions, and a thin grey line is the secondary graphic. The pale warm-grey paper colour is this author's example, not the definition of the style. What defines the style is the medium: one dense ink plus its own dilutions, a visibly fibrous paper ground, and the halo being the same ink diluted rather than a shadow or a new hue. No seal colour or other chroma appears in seconds 1–8. For new subjects, the paper can be cool grey, blue-grey, pale celadon, unbleached kraft or a dark charcoal sheet. On a dark sheet, invert to pale ink or gofun white and keep tonal dilution as the second value. An optional single restrained accent, such as a vermilion seal, should only be added if the subject justifies it. Recheck caption contrast after any change, because the low-contrast grey captions are already near the readability limit.

sources.style_evidence: The opening scene is built from layered silhouettes (sun disc, black volcano, sea horizon) with limited colours and clear depth. The purple potato silhouette is reused as a wipe.
sources.palette_lesson: The colours are scene-driven, not a fixed recipe. The night title uses a near-black warm field lit by one amber sun. The daytime chapter switches to an amber/apricot gradient sky over dark brown soil. The amber in these frames is this author's example for a dawn/sunset and shochu-warmth subject, not a style constant. What should transfer is the structure: one dominant ambient field per chapter (dark night or a luminous gradient), one semantic subject colour reused for emphasis text and transition wipes (here plum = sweet potato), off-white or dark-brown type chosen for contrast against that field, and a single cool/neutral accent reserved for a process element (white water streaks). For new subjects, derive the field from the setting and process stage and recheck text contrast whenever the field flips from dark to light.

sources.style_evidence: Every shot relies on solid dark silhouettes: marching figures, rows of audience heads, pursuers. They read through outline and pose against backlit fields, with clear depth layers and almost no internal detail.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, cool slate and blue-gray world is this author's choice for an oppressive, broadcast-dystopia mood. It is not a fixed rule of the style. What defines the craft: (1) a narrow, low-saturation environment value range; (2) one dominant light source per shot (tunnel core, projection screen, ceiling strips) that sets the silhouettes; (3) exactly one saturated hue reserved for the protagonist or turning point, with matching local light spill. The orange-red accent is meaningful because nothing else in the frame is warm. For new subjects, change the environment's color family and keep the single complementary accent: deep teal-green sea cave with a coral accent; dusty violet desert dusk with a lime or acid-yellow accent; warm sepia factory haze with a cobalt accent; cold snow-white overcast field with dark figures and a crimson accent; murky olive jungle with a magenta accent. Recheck that the silhouettes still separate from the glow field, and that captions on bright surfaces keep their contrast.

sources.style_evidence: Handwritten brush-script lettering, cut notebook paper with uneven torn edges, tape strips and light shadows in a shared craft language. The layers are placed rather than wobbling continuously.
sources.palette_lesson: The base is a quiet, low-chroma desk/stage layer: here, a near-white map with gray-blue linework. White and off-white paper, black ink type, and small saturated accents (tape, pins, marker strokes, play button) carry the color. The color families (pale gray map, sky-blue/coral/purple/yellow tapes, orange marker) are this author's brand-specific example, not a rule. The style constraints are: (1) a subdued, low-contrast environmental ground that relates to the subject, (2) paper surfaces lighter than or distinct from that ground, with visible torn edges and soft shadows, (3) black or near-black ink for readable copy, (4) a limited set of saturated accents assigned to tape, pins and annotations, with one hot accent (orange) for emphasis strokes. The butter-cream full panel is a transition wipe, not the canvas.

sources.style_evidence: A tactile craft layer: headline tiles rotated slightly like cut labels, tape strips holding cards and notes, a sticky note, contact shadows, all on a grainy paper surface.
sources.palette_lesson: The warm kraft paper ground, espresso-brown type, caramel/amber emphasis and cream tiles are this author's palette for a coffee-shop example: the redesigned site and the stage share that palette on purpose. They are not a requirement of the style. What the style needs is a single textured matte surface as canvas, with a soft vignette. One dark ink handles headlines and step pills, one warm accent handles emphasized words, number dots and active buttons. A separate annotation-ink color goes to script and arrows, and props like sticky notes and tape carry their own prop colors. Embedded screen content keeps its own palette, and here a clashing 'before' palette was used deliberately against the harmonized 'after'. For a new subject, choose the surface color from the product or brand mood, then re-derive ink, accent and annotation colors so headline text and labels keep strong contrast against that surface and against any card they sit on.

sources.palette_lesson: The colours that define the style are the medium's own: a lightly textured paper canvas with fiber speckle and a soft vignette, matte opaque paper pieces in a limited set (about four to six families), a near-black rounded heavy display ink for text, and small muted geometric confetti. The author's specific colour choices (warm greige paper for the statement scene, mint/sage sky with yellow-green to forest-green hills, a mustard sun, navy and coral confetti, a lime highlighter) are one example tied to a growth and enablement subject. They are not fixed tokens. Note that the canvas tint already changes with the scene in this source, from warm off-white to cool mint, which shows the background is meant to follow the scene. In new projects, keep the paper grain, the matte cut-paper layers and the dark ink type, and choose the paper tint from the subject. sources.style_evidence: Every object is a flat cut or torn paper shape with a visible white paper-core edge and limited flat paper colors. There are no outlines, shapes are layered as stacked sheets, and the grain is uniform.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's colors belong to the subject and scene: a sky-blue sky band, a row of muted multicolor houses (teal, terracotta, ochre, slate blue, sand) and a kraft-tan street for an outdoor 1920s town, then teal striped wallpaper and reddish-brown wood for the lab. The background changes per scene, so there is no fixed canvas color. What defines the style is the medium: matte, slightly desaturated paper stocks, fine fiber grain, a white torn-paper core on every edge, flat fills without outlines, and a small set of ink colors for type (dark navy plus one crimson highlight, with pale grey for words not yet reached) on cream label strips. Keep the white tear rim readable against whatever field you choose. Light fields need a slightly darker paper behind the rim, or a soft contact shadow.

Shared movement quality: follow shared_motion_guidance and tech.motion_guidance. Design coherent trajectories, acceleration, transitions and settling with readable holds. Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

sources.style_evidence: A limited set of spot inks (fluorescent pink, blue, yellow, red-orange, green) on visible uncoated paper. Speckled grain and dropouts sit inside every ink fill. Overprints create new tones (blue over pink turns navy, pink over yellow turns orange). The texture stays stable across frames.
sources.palette_lesson: The style comes from the medium, not the specific hues. It needs a paper ground showing through, a handful of grainy spot inks, and overlaps that produce visible mixed tones. The pink, blue, yellow, red-orange and green set and the light warm-gray paper are this author's example choices; the evidence only measured a light warm-gray composite dominant. Use pink as the shape and pattern ink and yellow as the field ink. Give blue, red-orange and green to type, sized so each word reads clearly against whatever it sits on. For new subjects, swap the paper tone and the ink set to fit the scene and mood, but keep 2–4 inks, plausible overprint results, and readable text contrast.

sources.style_evidence: Every frame builds tone from dot size or density: the iris (1s), the floor band (3–5s), the magenta radial (6s), the dither blocks (7s) and the ring field (8s). There are almost no smooth gradients.
sources.palette_lesson: The constraint that defines the style is a strict two-or-three-ink system. One saturated spot colour, near-black and near-white swap figure/ground roles, and tone comes only from halftone dot density. The particular acid green, the single magenta title burst and the black terminal opening are this author's example (a brand-like choice), not requirements. What carries over is the polarity flips: dark emissive screen → light printed paper → accent colour promoted to full-bleed ground, with black type always as the key plate. For new subjects, pick one spot ink plus one contrast ink to suit the scene, keep a neutral dark or light partner, and make sure heavy type keeps contrast against the dot field wherever it is densest.

sources.style_evidence: The whole stage, the floor band and the confidence-bar fills are built from a consistent, regular halftone dot screen with clear outlines. Tone comes from dot density, and the dots stay anchored as the cards move.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's example is fully achromatic: a mid-charcoal halftone ground, black-ink objects with white keylines, off-white paper cards and white LED dots. A darker near-black overlay is used for the spotlight beat. The measured composite dominant shifts from mid grey (s1–6) to very dark grey (s7–8). That reflects the dimming overlay, not a second palette. What defines the style is not grey itself. It is the print constraint: tone made by dot density in one ink against a substrate, plus solid ink badges and stamps, with emphasis carried by luminance and inversion rather than hue. For new subjects the ground can be any single ink-on-substrate pairing that suits the scene. Keep paper cards (or the subject's equivalent) as the brightest plane. Reserve the darkest overlay for focus moments, and check that the small text on cards stays legible over the dot screen. If one accent is added, it should be a spot-ink color with a fixed semantic role (e.g., 'hit' state), not decoration.

sources.palette_lesson: The red-brown sepia monochrome here is this author's grading choice for a 'cursed vintage film / moon level' scene, not a requirement of the style. Measured composite dominance is only a near-black dark red, and it includes the curtains. The medium constraints that matter are structural. (1) Use one tinted tonal ramp: a dark ground, mid forms and pale highlights for effects, puffs and interactive items. (2) Reserve one saturated accent for the threat or focal point, here the red eyes, plus a tiny secondary accent such as the magenta target. (3) Let beams and light be translucent lighter values of the same family that let the hatching show through, not new hues. For new subjects, keep the single-ramp-plus-one-accent logic and choose the tint from the scene. For example: cold blue-gray moonlit monochrome for a night ocean, olive-green sepia for a swamp or jungle stage, a teal-cyan ramp with an orange accent for an underwater level, smoky violet for a haunted carnival, faded mustard-ochre for a desert daytime set, or a neutral silver-gray film look with a single red accent. Recheck that the accent and the HUD stay readable against whichever dark or light ground you pick.

tech.implementation: Preprocess high-contrast imagery, fixed photocopy grain, torn edges, and cut lettering. Composite page layouts with deliberate paste and page-turn actions.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.

Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. 2. Write a short storyboard with explicit time ranges. Give each section one main idea, a clear focal point, and enough reading or observation time. Framework contract: select the packages, runtime, timeline registration, validation commands, and renderer that actually belong to {{render_pipeline}}. Do not mix another framework's hooks, composition lifecycle, or renderer. Specialist modeling, photography, drawing, and scientific computation can produce inputs for the selected video framework without being replaced by it.
Palette contract: read palette before implementation. Use its suggested tokens only when task, brand, or reference colors are absent. Keep supplied exact colors, source artwork, existing semantic assignments, and style color-family and color-count constraints unchanged. Use chroma-js to validate and normalize equivalent color values, select readable existing foreground/background pairs, and interpolate only when palette.gradient is enabled. Do not recolor assets or add hues to improve contrast; change text placement, an existing backing color, or typography instead. Follow palette.agent_instruction and inspect actual composited frames.
Shared movement quality: follow shared_motion_guidance and tech.motion_guidance. Design coherent trajectories, acceleration, transitions and settling with readable holds. Use time-based interpolation and authored easing when appropriate; preserve deliberate cuts, impacts, stepped exposure, whole-pixel placement and line-boil cadence. Do not automatically add springs, bounce, floating or extra in-between poses. Derive state from composition time; bake or deterministically replay any stateful smoothing, physics or camera damping. Verify direct, backward and out-of-order seeks plus the decoded sequence and loop seams. Keep the existing palette and style-specific motion direction intact.
Production ownership: follow production_policy. Choose the style_renderer and motion_engine from the style and motion requirements first, and state the selected tools and their responsibilities. Build the visuals and movement with those tools according to tech.implementation and visual_cues. Use {{render_pipeline}} only for scene assembly, seekable composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and export. Keep specialist rendering and motion logic in their own layers; do not substitute generic framework text, DOM transitions, or framework animation helpers merely because the pipeline is available. Native DOM or SVG is appropriate when it actually satisfies the style. Integrate deterministic time-driven layers or baked assets, and verify representative visuals and motion before assembling the full video.
Audio direction: follow audio_direction. Based on {{subject}}, {{audience_and_objective}}, the storyboard, visual_cues, and motion direction, suggest suitable background music, voiceover, sung vocals, sound effects, ambience, or silence. Honor {{audio_or_rhythm_requirements}} first. State the proposed choices and why they fit this topic and style; suggest mood, texture, energy, tempo where useful, voice language and delivery where useful, and scene-level audio changes. Do not impose a fixed soundtrack rule or include every layer. Source or create authorized assets, then use {{render_pipeline}} for assembly, synchronization, mixing, and export. Verify speech intelligibility, audio balance, absence of clipping, and picture synchronization in the final video.

motion_references.selection_policy: Optional candidates are screened for natural style compatibility. Before selection, inspect the actual scene illustration, assets, geometry and narrative beat. Keep only references whose defining action is supported by that scene. Choosing no reference is valid. Do not infer motion from a similar label; do not replace the existing style motion direction.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider a fixed hero stage whose internal composition separates, expands, and shifts from centered to peripheral copy without a cut. Adapt the example objects to the topic. Pin the stage rather than freezing every internal subject.

Consider anchored cards progressively covered by incoming cards, with optional scale or dimming for recession and a defined stack release. Keep active content readable and simulate sticky or pinned behavior with time-driven layers in video.

Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Consider meaningful narrative steps with synchronized copy and visual states, plus optional within-step progress or sticky graphics. Use only scene-level motions that serve the story, and schedule the same states by time for video.

Cutout headline words can disperse and recompose within photocopied page logic. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

A printed punctuation crop can connect page changes without modern glow. Optional only when actual scene assets support the defining action; preserve the style palette and medium and choose no reference when unsuitable.

Cut between designed photocopy headline pages with monochrome and an optional accent; preserve cut edges and grain rather than substituting clean neon fills. Optional only when concise text serves the actual scene; use approved colors and preserve this style’s visual rules.

Toner-heavy headline glyphs can choke shut into a solid photocopy block that becomes the next page's panel, keeping a ragged letter rim. Optional only for heavy display type; keep monochrome grain and do not substitute a clean rectangle wipe.

motion_references.agent_instruction: Read the actual illustration and complete pattern description, motion_sequence and video_adaptation. Identify which scene elements implement that action. Reject unsupported geometry, absent subjects, unintended depth, broken contact points or unrelated interactions. Select none when no candidate fits; use restrained style-native motion instead. Preserve authored transforms, fixed backgrounds and reading layers.

sources.style_evidence: Every object is a glossy emoji-style illustration with a consistent thick white die-cut border and a soft shadow or glow, placed with slight rotation. The same stickers come back as a scattered collection at second 6.
sources.palette_lesson: The core palette is a neutral light ground with near-black type and one saturated orange used for emphasis. Each scene then switches to its own solid full-bleed field (peach, orange, near-black, butter yellow, with a pale-mint wipe), and type flips between black and white to keep contrast on each field. The specific hues are this author's example for a city-deals theme. They are not constraints of the medium. What defines the style: one flat untextured field per beat; strong value contrast between field and type; glossy multicolour stickers kept apart from any field by a thick white border; an optional soft halo in a colour taken from the sticker; and one consistent accent colour for emphasised words. For new subjects, choose the field colours from the subject's mood. Keep a dark scene in the sequence for rhythm, and check white-border contrast on light fields; the border carries less contrast there, so a glow or shadow is needed.

sources.style_evidence: Pixel characters and the smiley badge have consistent thick white die-cut sticker borders and sit on a graph-paper notebook surface and a torn paper floor (s4-s8).
sources.palette_lesson: The grid stays in every frame and the accent roles stay fixed: one hot accent (magenta) is used as backing paper, halftone and stamp ink; black and white carry type and characters; cobalt blue and mustard yellow appear only rarely as third accents (one tile, one scrap, the blob's offset rim, the smiley). Scenes alternate between loud and quiet. Headline beats flood the frame with pink, and dialogue beats drop back to the plain grid so the bubbles can be read. The specific colours (sage graph paper, hot pink) belong to this author's example. They are not style constants. What defines the style is a light ruled/grid substrate, black-and-white cutout and pixel figures, one saturated print-ink accent, and white sticker borders that separate figures from any background.

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

sources.palette_lesson: The colours that belong to this example are the gold-ochre sky, the blue-and-white water, green grass and cypresses, a red border, and white, red and orange figures. These are a classic Early Christian or Byzantine-flavoured choice for a pastoral dove-and-fish subject, not a requirement of the style. The constraints that do define the medium are a limited set of discrete tile colours, each with small value jitter from tile to tile, dark grout lines, high-key reflective tiles (gold or glass) used sparingly for glints, and a neutral setting wall around the panel. New subjects should choose their own field colour: deep lapis or midnight blue with gold stars for night or sacred scenes; terracotta and umber stone tesserae for Roman floor mosaics; sea-green and turquoise glass for marine or poolside topics; black-and-white marble for architectural or geometric themes; or emerald and jade for gardens. The surround can be a cool slate, warm limestone, a dark wet-stone grout, or a dim church-interior shadow. Keep enough value contrast between the figure tiles and the field that silhouettes read at tile resolution.
