sources.palette_lesson: The colours come from the lighting state, not from a fixed swatch. In this example the time of day sets the palette: hazy noon in grey-blue and teal, golden hour in amber with dark olive ground, dusk in violet-grey sky with a red horizon, and night with warm torch pools on cream sand. The medium's constant is the material set (matte pixel-textured blocks, translucent refractive water, line-like glass, emissive torches). The author's own choices are the beach and sea subject, the teal water and the sunset sequence. A new subject should get its own environment and light: a cold blue-white snowfield at dawn, a dim cave lit by blue-green crystals, a misty forest under overcast light, a desert at noon with bleached sky and ochre blocks, or a night town of grey stone with sodium-orange lamps. Keep the overlay UI (dark translucent panels, one warm accent for sliders and buttons) separate from the world palette, and recheck its contrast against each lighting state.

sources.style_evidence: The whole world is built from consistent-size cubes: blocky chickens, cube trees, stepped terrain, block clouds and fence posts. Depth comes from flat-shaded faces and colour blocks.
sources.palette_lesson: The dominant green (the measured composite is a mid grass-green) comes from this example's subject, a daytime grassland biome. It is not a style constant. The UI accent green and the hearts are this author's choices. Keep the overlay neutral-dark and pick its accent to contrast with whatever biome is behind it.

Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. tech.implementation:
Background #F4ECD9. Rounded procedural hero (e.g. a capsule chest or gem) built with Three.js. MeshToonMaterial bases use foreground #26394A, accent_1 #547E8F and accent_2 #BA7461, with a 3-step DataTexture gradientMap (NearestFilter, NoColorSpace) and one fixed directional light. Outlines: render a normal+depth MRT/target, then a GLSL ShaderPass in EffectComposer detects depth/normal discontinuities and draws a constant pixel-width #26394A contour, scaled to output resolution. No backface scaling. OutputPass is used with tone mapping off so the bands keep their approved values. One paused GSAP timeline (registered with HyperFrames) owns the hero transform, a rarity uniform and the camera. 3-second preview of the reward recipe: idle sway 0–0.6s → rarity step (discrete material/rim/background tone swap) 0.6–1.2s → charge squash 1.2–1.8s → burst 1.8–2.1s → isolated reveal with glow card behind the hero → settle and hold by 3s. Burst particles are seeded and sit outside the silhouette. Any number label is HTML with data-reveal-after on its card. Each frame is rendered on seek from timeline time. Full video extends the stages and adds a collection step.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider bounded pupil following with optional delayed brows, slight head tilt, and scheduled blinks. Require suitable facial layers or a rig, preserve expression and drawing cadence, and do not interpret this as viewer eye tracking.

sources.style_evidence: The plane and clouds are 3D forms with discrete, stepped shadow bands (violet shadow, lilac mid, peach rim) and flat matte fills. Light direction stays consistent through the camera rolls, and there are no realistic reflections.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's colours here are a scene choice, not a medium rule. A cool indigo night-sky opening changes into a golden-orange and magenta sunset over a plum sea. Clouds are violet with peach rim light, and the hero object is cream with a small red/green/white livery. The colours that define the style are relational: (1) a few discrete shadow bands per form, with shadows in a saturated hue-shifted colour rather than grey; (2) environmental light carries the warmth while object colours stay flat and matte; (3) one light-valued hero against a darker or more saturated environment, so it always reads; (4) white serif type over mid-to-dark areas. For new subjects, take the background from the setting and time of day. Options include a teal-and-sea-green morning ocean with coral cloud rims; a pale cyan noon sky with blue-grey shadows; a slate storm field with acid-green lightning-lit edges; a desert ochre ground with rust shadows; a snowy blue-white valley with lilac shadow bands; or a deep forest-green dusk with amber rims. Re-check text contrast as the lighting moves: the white serif works on indigo, plum and orange midtones, but needs a darker local area or a slight shadow when bright clouds or sky pass behind it, as nearly happens at 8 s.

sources.style_evidence: The cat has consistent dark outlines, flat fills and discrete shadow bands while sitting in a 3D space. Its outline width and lighting stay stable across cuts at 2, 3, 4, 5 and 8 seconds.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors here belong to this author's chosen subject and setting: an orange tabby, pastel coral, teal and lavender facades, saturated toy-car colors, a blue-grey road and a hazy pale sky. None of them is a requirement of the style. What defines the style is a set of role relationships. First, the hero character carries the most saturated warm hue plus a dark outline. Second, the ground plane is a mid-value, low-chroma field that the hero contrasts against. Third, props and vehicles supply small, distinct saturated accents. Fourth, distance is shown by lightening values toward the horizon. The close-up at 3 seconds shows the author dropping hue contrast (an orange cat against an ochre wall) and relying on the outline for separation. The full-frame amber at 7 seconds shows a scene-specific color field, not a canvas color. For new subjects, keep these role relationships and pick colors that suit the scene. Avoid a fixed warm or cream recipe, and recheck hero-to-ground contrast in every shot.

tech.implementation:
Browser preview: neutral #F0EDE5 studio sweep with a procedural PMREM RoomEnvironment. A PBR object (brushed metal and a MeshPhysicalMaterial glass with transmission/IOR) sits on a plane with PCF soft shadows and contact shadows. Renderer output is SRGB with ACES tone mapping configured explicitly, plus a restrained BokehPass depth of field and OutputPass. A GSAP timeline owns a measured dolly/arc camera and an object settle with plausible eased acceleration and no floating. 3s preview: slow 10° arc with a focus pull. Optional caustic recipe: an offscreen render target samples the background for a refraction approximation, and any projected caustic texture is tied to surface and light motion and labeled as an approximation, not path-traced. Full video: the implementation calls for Blender PBR, Cycles and baked simulation. That capability is not available, so this is reported as missing; if installed, render via bpy/Cycles to a transparent_png_sequence, check denoise stability, and composite in HyperFrames.
Optional recipe caustic_optics: Validate reflected/refracted silhouettes and transmitted light together. Water caustics on receiver geometry must move consistently with the surface and lighting, not slide as unrelated decoration. Use offline path-traced assets when the chosen browser renderer cannot provide the optical effect. Identify approximations; do not call projected patterns physically traced caustics.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Three.js PBR gives a faithful, deterministic, bounded approximation for a 3-second preview. It cannot provide traced caustics, so those claims are avoided. Soft_surface_lighting is a near-duplicate recipe and its practices are folded in. Blender/Cycles is the stated full-quality route but is unavailable, and that is disclosed rather than silently substituted. Fallback tokens apply only to presentation elements.

sources.style_evidence: Every frame shows a photoreal planet render: believable cloud albedo, night-side city emission, a correct terminator and atmospheric limb scattering, with a measured, near-static camera.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black field here is driven by the subject: it is literally outer space, not a style requirement. The fixed parts of the method are luminance and color roles. The background stays the darkest, quietest value. The hero subject's palette comes from its real materials (blue ocean and atmosphere, white clouds, warm amber artificial light confined to the night side). Data particles are small neutral points with no bloom. Text is a single high-contrast neutral overlay. Warm versus cool is semantic: warm means human activity or emission, cool means natural light and atmosphere. For a new subject, choose the environment a photoreal camera would actually see, then keep the same hierarchy: a quiet background, a materially lit hero, a sparse neutral data layer, and one rare emissive accent.

sources.style_evidence: Plausible planetary lighting: one directional sun, a soft terminator, atmospheric rim scattering, ocean sheen, layered clouds and emissive night lights. These read as a credible physical render, not a stylised one.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black blue-violet starfield is this author's choice for a space subject. It is not a rule of the style. What actually defines the style is a dark or low-key stage that lets the atmospheric rim and emissive lights read, a single warm/cool light split (cool blue rim and ocean against warm peach terminator haze and amber city lights), and one saturated accent colour (amber) kept for UI state and key numbers. For other subjects, the background should come from the physical environment and its lighting, with the warm/cool split adjusted to that light. Keep UI text high-contrast against whatever sits behind it, and keep a single accent tied to interaction rather than decoration.

tech.implementation:
Background #111C29. About 30–60k Points whose BufferGeometry attributes hold seeded fixed samples: pose A position (e.g. a sphere), pose B (a recognizable silhouette such as a bird or logo shape sampled from a procedural SDF), a per-particle seed, and a color role (#65BEC2 cool body, #CEAF79 warm focal accent, #EFF5EE highlights). The vertex shader computes position = mix(A, B, ease(uMorph, staggered by seed)) plus analytic curl-like offsets from uTime, and size/brightness from density. The fragment shader draws soft discs with additive blending capped by alpha. UnrealBloomPass with a high threshold and low strength keeps edges readable. GSAP's paused timeline sets uTime, uMorph and uTrail uniforms; nothing is integrated per frame, so seeks are exact. 3s preview: drift 0–0.8s → flow into the silhouette 0.8–2.0s → stable hold 2.0–3.0s. Fireworks recipe: birth times and velocities are seeded, and trajectories are analytic (p0 + v·t + ½g·t²) in the shader with fading trails from sampled earlier times.
Optional recipe particle_spectacle: Plan emission, ascent, burst expansion, fading trails, environmental light and a deliberate finale. Use deterministic birth times, seeded velocities and analytic or baked trajectories; retain foreground clarity and stationary background. Do not multiply identical small bursts or use full-screen glow to conceal weak choreography.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Shader-evaluated analytic motion is the implementation's explicit method and stays deterministic under any seek. GLSL owns per-particle motion and GSAP owns the uniforms, so each property has one owner. Canvas, p5 and PixiJS were rejected because they lose depth and efficient GPU bloom. InstancedMesh is heavier than Points. Bloom is bounded so glow never erases the silhouette.

sources.style_evidence: Brass and cream analog instruments (telescope, gimbal rings, rotary lens wheel) with an observatory or lab-apparatus look, set against modern UI.

A dystopian, mid-century-style vision of the future: a monitor on a stem, a broadcast face on a giant screen, uniform marching masses, a concrete corridor. Mechanical and broadcast display language rather than neon grids.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-black, cool slate and blue-gray world is this author's choice for an oppressive, broadcast-dystopia mood. It is not a fixed rule of the style. What defines the craft: (1) a narrow, low-saturation environment value range; (2) one dominant light source per shot (tunnel core, projection screen, ceiling strips) that sets the silhouettes; (3) exactly one saturated hue reserved for the protagonist or turning point, with matching local light spill. The orange-red accent is meaningful because nothing else in the frame is warm. For new subjects, change the environment's color family and keep the single complementary accent: deep teal-green sea cave with a coral accent; dusty violet desert dusk with a lime or acid-yellow accent; warm sepia factory haze with a cobalt accent; cold snow-white overcast field with dark figures and a crimson accent; murky olive jungle with a magenta accent. Recheck that the silhouettes still separate from the glow field, and that captions on bright surfaces keep their contrast.

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. sources.style_evidence: Seconds 1–3 show a circular glass lens that visibly magnifies and distorts the card text beneath it, with a rim highlight and curved rim lettering. This is real refraction, not plain blur.
sources.palette_lesson:
These colours are the author's own example. Cyan-to-violet light gradients, an aqua-to-deep-teal field and then a near-black charcoal stage are scene and brand choices that move from light to dark across the acts. They are not rules of the style. The rules are these:
- Keep one cool ambient field per act behind neutral UI surfaces: white frosted, charcoal opaque or smoked translucent.
- Reserve a single saturated interactive accent (here teal) for selection, send and active states.
- Let embedded media (warm reds, photos/renders) bring the only warm colour.
- Use small semantic status colours (green waveform, orange playhead, violet active outline) sparingly on dark tiles.
For new subjects, choose the field from mood and brand. Examples: a warm coral-to-magenta for lifestyle or creator apps, a deep forest-to-moss for finance or sustainability, a graphite-to-steel-blue for developer tools, a pale mint-to-white daylight field for health, or an inky plum-to-black for a night or entertainment mood. Keep the accent hue distinct from the field and check text contrast on every translucent panel.

sources.style_evidence: The bowl's glass refracts the striped wall and red band into curved, wrapped bands (most visible at seconds 1, 2 and 8), with rim highlights and a visible boundary. The room behind stays recognizable through the glass.
sources.palette_lesson: The palette has three layers. First, the set: a room of navy/off-white stripes, a red band, a dark green wainscot and a black/white checkerboard floor, with a warm brown wooden table. Second, the medium: clear glass and a cool teal-cyan water tint. Third, the saturated accents: orange-red, yellow, blue and orange-white fish against a pale pebble floor. The room colors are this author's example set dressing. Their strong graphic contrast is there to make the refraction easy to see, so they are not a fixed palette. What defines the style is: a neutral-to-graphic backdrop with enough pattern or contrast for glass distortion to read, a tinted transparent medium that stays distinct from the backdrop, and small high-chroma subjects inside it. The dominant colors measured from these frames (warm greys and tans, near-black) come from the wood, the top-down floor views and the dark capture border. They are not a background recipe.

sources.style_evidence: Second 8 is an isometric cutaway room on consistent axes, with desks in a diagonal row, tonal top and side faces, no perspective shrinkage, and data on in-world boards.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's palette is scene-driven. The exterior uses a cool, low-key night (navy sky, layered dark teal-green forests, near-black ground) with a single pale moon. Warm amber appears only as a story signal, when the house-character's windows light up. Contrast with the subject comes from value (the off-white head against a dark field) and from warm against cool. The cream radial glow at 7s is a light-transition effect, not a canvas colour. The interior at 8s switches to a near-black void around a dark plum-brown isometric room, and saturated hue-coded roofs (orange, lavender, teal, yellow) separate the characters. What should transfer: a dominant environmental colour family with tonal-step depth, a light-valued hero with one or two signature hues reused across its parts (here teal), restrained warm emissive accents tied to events, and categorical hue-coding for ensemble characters. The navy/teal night recipe and the specific roof colours are this video's example, not constraints of the style.

sources.style_evidence: Mostly consistent oblique axes, a limited muted palette and light shadows. It is weaker than the others because the render is real 3D with a perspective camera, not flat illustration.
sources.palette_lesson: The near-white page and dark browser frame are screen-recording context (website UI), not a style background. The composition's real palette is inside the map: muted lawn green, soft grey roads, slate-blue water, and buildings in desaturated pastels (cream, blush pink, lilac, blue-grey) with charcoal factory roofs and brick chimneys. One warm orange/amber accent family marks the active state and tags. These colors are this author's choice for a sunny daytime suburban town, and the app even offers Morning/Dusk/Night modes. What defines the style is the medium: flat matte shading with no textures, a restrained desaturated base with one saturated accent hue for interaction or emphasis, soft ambient shadows, and readable 2D labels on top. For new subjects, take the ground plane and lighting from the scene rather than reusing green lawn and white UI.

styles.visual_cues: Use rounded forms, restrained handmade surface detail, matte materials, broad lights, and credible contact shadows. Keep colors limited. Animate weight and slight elasticity without continuous melting; distinguish the digital surface treatment from actual clay stop motion.

tech.implementation: Create rounded meshes, matte materials, and broad lighting in Blender. Use controlled deformation and keyframes; describe the result as a clay-like 3D treatment when no physical clay was filmed.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.

sources.style_evidence: The second ident's cloud and sun are rounded, matte, broadly lit forms with a soft contact shadow and limited colors: a clay/toy-like digital surface.
sources.palette_lesson: The colors are set per ident to fit the brand personality, not by a medium rule. Ident A's black space with a warm gold radial glow, a champagne crystal and off-white type is this author's example for a 'premium/cosmic' mood. Ident B's sky-blue sweep with a white cloud, a single warm sun accent and saturated blue type fits a 'friendly pocket' mood. What the style itself requires: a seamless, non-textured stage (void or studio sweep) whose luminance falls off radially toward the edges to frame one centered hero; one dominant hue family for the stage; the hero lifted from the stage by value contrast (bright on dark, or white with soft shading on mid-tone); one complementary accent (gold rings, a yellow sun); and type colored so it stays readable against the local background behind it, i.e. off-white on dark, saturated mid-blue on the pale lower gradient. New subjects should pick the stage hue from their own world and keep this hero/stage/accent luminance structure.

sources.style_evidence: The ivory scene's rounded capsules and fruit read as matte soft-plastic/clay 3D with broad light and credible contact shadows. The Orbiel sphere is also matte and soft.
sources.palette_lesson: This is a multi-brand logo-reveal reel. The palette is chosen per brand and per scene, not fixed. Each segment has its own atmosphere: cosmic navy with amber emissive accents for a connectivity/space idea, warm ivory with red/green food accents for a food brand, and black with chrome and cool rim light for automotive. These specific hues are the author's examples. The constants are structural: one quiet low-detail gradient field per scene (a radial vignette brightening toward the subject), one dominant material for the mark, and one or two small saturated accents. Type colors are matched to the field (white on dark, warm brown on ivory). Glow and highlights stay confined to small points or rims. When adapting to new subjects, derive the field from the subject's world and keep high subject/field contrast. Re-check the type contrast whenever the field changes.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider depth-dependent miniature-scene parallax with separate rear, foreground, and optional highlight responses. A flick-triggered creature hop is optional and requires suitable assets. Preserve projection, contact, occlusion, and fixed reading layers.

Consider a full camera circuit around a stationary subject with angle-specific annotations and a closing front view. Require complete geometry or sufficient captured turntable views. Omit when strict isometric projection or a single flat image cannot support it; character travel around a center is a different pattern.

Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Consider meaningful narrative steps with synchronized copy and visual states, plus optional within-step progress or sticky graphics. Use only scene-level motions that serve the story, and schedule the same states by time for video.
Only when the scene contains separable components and the reveal explains their relationships. Do not explode arbitrary decorative shapes.
Use real depth geometry or a clearly identified 2.5D approximation. Do not translate a camera through a flat illustration and call it a dolly.
Requires real 3D depth or an explicitly labeled parallax alternative. Orbit the camera, not the subject; avoid uncontrolled full rotations.

Use Lighting State Progression when time of day, weather or world state advances the story. Preserve this style’s material grammar and fixed environmental anchors; coordinate lighting, shadows, reflections and state-owned accents. Keep approved base material colors and medium limits. An authored front is optional; do not infer its precise method from source stills.

Use a diorama built as a free-standing island or plinth that is finished on all four sides, not a front-only theatre box. Keep the elevated camera height, fixed target at the diorama center and restrained depth of field so models and paths stay sharp. Local actions may continue, but the base doesn't move. Check that no unfinished cut edges show at the rear.

sources.style_evidence: A complete miniature stadium and neighbourhood seen from an elevated oblique view. Architecture, cars and trees share consistent scales. Small local details read clearly and nothing is blurred away.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's colors come from the subject's materials (grass green, brick red, concrete off-white, slate roofs) and from a dark-navy app UI that frames the scene. The UI's dark chrome and the cool slate haze are this author's product skin. They are not a requirement of the style. What defines the style is a set of restrained, desaturated real-world material colors on matte flat-shaded meshes, with one saturated focal surface (the pitch) that holds the eye, and a separate high-contrast UI/label layer (dark pills with white text, white selected chips) that stays readable on top of busy geometry. For new subjects, set the surround from the scene's own lighting mode: daylight neutral, sunset warm, or night with emissive accents. Then pick one saturated focal material, keep the context buildings muted, and recheck label contrast against whatever ground sits under each capsule.

sources.style_evidence: A complete miniature-feeling fantasy building set inside a bounded ring of trees, with consistent prop scales, an elevated oblique orbiting view and depth falloff from fog. Small local action (the wisp, the smoke) plays across the environment.
sources.palette_lesson: The palette here belongs to this particular scene: a daylight fantasy meadow (yellow-green and mid-green grass and trees, pale grey-white fog), a building in stone grey-brown, cream timber, terracotta and red roofs and slate-blue towers, with warm amber emissive windows and one pale cyan-white light accent. The measured dominant colours (light grey, dark green) are just the fog and foliage averaged together; they are not a canvas or design token. The style itself depends on how colour is used, not on these particular hues. Atmospheric depth fog that matches the sky or ambient light, one warm emissive accent family that contrasts with the ambient tone, one small cool 'guide' light that moves, and saturated local colours that get lighter and less saturated with distance. For a new subject, choose the ground, sky and fog from the setting and the time of day. Keep the warm-emissive-against-ambient contrast, and check that the guide light still stands out against whatever it passes over.

Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. sources.style_evidence: The character is a jointed paper puppet with separate hat, head, torso, limbs and suitcase. It moves through hinged pose replacement (stride at 2s, step at 5s, expression swap at 6s), and a torn paper sheet acts as the scene wipe.
sources.palette_lesson: This author's colors belong to the subject and scene: a sky-blue sky band, a row of muted multicolor houses (teal, terracotta, ochre, slate blue, sand) and a kraft-tan street for an outdoor 1920s town, then teal striped wallpaper and reddish-brown wood for the lab. The background changes per scene, so there is no fixed canvas color. What defines the style is the medium: matte, slightly desaturated paper stocks, fine fiber grain, a white torn-paper core on every edge, flat fills without outlines, and a small set of ink colors for type (dark navy plus one crimson highlight, with pale grey for words not yet reached) on cream label strips. Keep the white tear rim readable against whatever field you choose. Light fields need a slightly darker paper behind the rim, or a soft contact shadow.

sources.style_evidence: Photographic portrait cutout with a white cut edge, torn-paper cards, tape and lettering arranged around one theme. The pieces are placed and recomposed, with soft contact shadows.
sources.palette_lesson: The base is a quiet, low-chroma desk/stage layer: here, a near-white map with gray-blue linework. White and off-white paper, black ink type, and small saturated accents (tape, pins, marker strokes, play button) carry the color. The color families (pale gray map, sky-blue/coral/purple/yellow tapes, orange marker) are this author's brand-specific example, not a rule. The style constraints are: (1) a subdued, low-contrast environmental ground that relates to the subject, (2) paper surfaces lighter than or distinct from that ground, with visible torn edges and soft shadows, (3) black or near-black ink for readable copy, (4) a limited set of saturated accents assigned to tape, pins and annotations, with one hot accent (orange) for emphasis strokes. The butter-cream full panel is a transition wipe, not the canvas.

sources.palette_lesson: This author's example uses an oxblood velvet curtain frame, a peach-to-amber sunset backdrop, taupe-to-brown haze layers, near-black silhouettes, a dark placard with cream serif text, and tiny warm window and bulb lights. The hues are a scene choice (sunset, home, nostalgia), not a rule of the style. The medium rules are these. First, one luminous backdrop field behind flat opaque dark silhouettes. Second, depth made only by stepping value toward the horizon. Third, detail shown as negative cutouts or lit openings in the dark mass. Fourth, a small set of colors with one warm accent reserved for light sources. Fifth, high contrast between text and its board. The curtain or proscenium color can change with the setting (navy, forest green, black, plum). The backdrop can be any luminous field that suits the subject, as long as the silhouettes stay clearly darker and the caption board keeps its contrast.

What actually defines the style is the medium: matte, low-sheen clay pigment in a small set of saturated colors (primary red, yellow and blue for props, warm skin tones, grey and charcoal for clothing) shown against one plain, single-hue painted backdrop so the clay shapes stand out clearly. What the style needs: readable contrast between the tile material and the surface it sits on, one clear light direction, and colour from physical props. Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Explain which choices support this particular video; do not assign a fixed genre, tempo, instrument, voice, or mandatory audio layer to the style.
suggestion_dimensions: Whether background music is useful, and its suggested mood, texture, energy, tempo range, and progression.
Whether voiceover helps explain the topic, and its suggested language, tone, pace, and placement.
Whether sung vocals support the topic or distract from narration and essential text.
Whether sound effects, ambience, or silence clarify key actions, transitions, and reading holds.
How audio changes across scenes, supports motion cadence, and leaves space for speech and comprehension.
audio_direction.selection_guidance: Treat these as task-specific suggestions, not requirements to include every audio layer. Honor explicit user audio choices and supplied assets. When inputs are absent, propose a coherent direction and state assumptions; do not silently default to instrumental music or invent available audio assets.
audio_direction.integration_guidance: Select or create authorized audio assets separately from visual construction and motion design. Use render_pipeline to assemble, synchronize, mix, and export audio with picture. Keep speech intelligible, avoid clipping and competing vocals, and inspect the delivered audio and picture together.

suggested_combinations.selection_guidance: Rotoscoping needs verified live-action reference and has no listed renderer; without footage, report the gap. Use it alone for realistic traced motion, and choose a hybrid for a print-texture fill language or explanatory line overlays.

supporting_styles.role: Fill treatment: two-ink risograph grain and fixed registration offset

suggestions.rationale: A riso fill gives traced footage a distinctive printed look and constrains fills to a stable limited set, which suppresses frame-to-frame color noise.
suggestions.best_for: Music videos, documentary vignettes and editorial films from supplied footage.
suggestions.video_application: Trace contours in #314249 and fill with #9D8A72 as the second ink on #F1EBDD, using fixed grain and a constant registration offset.
suggestions.html_application: Canvas plays the traced sequence with a static grain texture; step controls work by keyboard and reduced motion shows a key frame.
consistency_rules: Primary tokens act as the two inks; drop riso's blue and coral.
Grain and offset stay fixed, never per-frame.
Use the same simplification rules on every frame.

supporting_styles.role: Explanatory overlay: animated motion paths and joint markers

suggestions.rationale: Line-art paths over traced figures can reveal movement mechanics, such as trajectories or angles, for sports or dance analysis.
suggestions.best_for: Biomechanics, sports technique and dance instruction.
suggestions.video_application: After a traced pass, draw trajectory paths and angle arcs in #9D8A72, holding on the key position.
suggestions.html_application: SVG overlay toggled by a labeled control; values are announced as text, and the scrubber is keyboard-accessible.
consistency_rules: Overlay strokes thinner than contours.
Paths derive from traced positions, not invented ones.
One accent for analysis marks.

styles.visual_cues: Separate character artwork into rigged parts with defined joints, pivots, occlusion, motion limits, and replaceable expressions. Animate poses, arcs, anticipation, and settling; draw replacement poses when needed. Avoid excessive stretch, exposed joint seams, or claiming every frame was redrawn.
styles.note: A supplemental design reference; not claimed as a directly named style in the source collection. Rigged part movement is distinct from independent frame-by-frame drawing.

tech.implementation: Define parent-child transforms, pivots, and layer order. Sequence rigged part movement and use replacement artwork for exceptional poses.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

motion_guidance.application: Apply shared movement quality to 2D Rigged Animation without weakening its visual_cues, materials, typography or existing motion_references.
motion_guidance.cadence_guidance: Use smooth, coherent authored movement where the action benefits from it. Preserve deliberate sharp cuts, impacts, constant-speed sections and reading holds; not every transition needs easing.
motion_guidance.implementation: Prefer existing timeline and renderer dependencies. Evaluate key states at requested composition time, maintain a single property owner, and cache or deterministically replay stateful motion. Do not introduce a library solely to add generic smoothing.

style_renderer.selection_basis: Use visual_cues and tech.implementation for styles, or the selected style and this pattern implementation for motion recipes. Select by visual fidelity and medium, not pipeline availability.

motion_engine.selection_basis: Use the authored action, style cadence, trajectory, material behavior, and simulation requirements. Select one owner for each animated property.

styles.executable_prompt_template:
Replace all double-brace placeholders with task inputs before execution. Use documented defaults only for omitted optional inputs and state the assumptions.
Create a 2D Rigged Animation video about {{subject}} for {{audience_and_objective}}. Use {{assets_and_exact_copy}}. Deliver a video of {{duration_seconds}} seconds, with aspect ratio {{aspect_ratio}}, resolution {{resolution}}, and frame rate {{frame_rate}}. Follow {{audio_or_rhythm_requirements}} and save deliverables to {{output_directory}}.
Use {{render_pipeline}} for composition and export only. If omitted, resolve it to tech.framework_selection.default. 1. Inspect the project, available tools, assets, exact wording, and input formats. Reuse suitable existing components. Treat visual_cues as art-direction constraints and choose only the tech.recommended_stack entries needed for the selected framework and asset-generation method. Example dimensions, palette sizes, beats, and scenes apply only when the task adopts them.
2. Write a short storyboard with explicit time ranges. Give each section one main idea, a clear focal point, and enough reading or observation time. Plan staging around this style's visual rules: Separate character artwork into rigged parts with defined joints, pivots, occlusion, motion limits, and replaceable expressions. Animate poses, arcs, anticipation, and settling; draw replacement poses when needed. Avoid excessive stretch, exposed joint seams, or claiming every frame was redrawn. Add secondary styles only when their materials, composition, and movement remain compatible.
3. Implement the style-specific technique: Define parent-child transforms, pivots, and layer order. Sequence rigged part movement and use replacement artwork for exceptional poses. Keep Canvas, DOM, and WebGL in the browser and file processing in Node.js or Python. Drive visual updates from shared, seekable video time; load fonts and assets, seed randomness, and cache stateful simulation. Centralize colors, fonts, dimensions, camera settings, and timing. Build representative frames and key actions before expanding the sequence.
4. Follow only the tech.render_pipeline route for {{render_pipeline}}. Distinguish drawing or pose-exposure rate from delivery frame rate. Use task-provided or authorized audio, and synchronize picture and sound against the same time data. Match composition and velocity at loop boundaries.
5. Render and inspect actual opening, key-action, transition, and closing frames, then watch the decoded video. Check the style-specific constraints in visual_cues, readable text, correct glyphs, stable materials and outlines, missing assets, crop margins, timing, dimensions, and audio synchronization. Fix issues and rerender until the relevant checks pass; compilation alone is insufficient.
6. Deliver the video, editable source or project, a key-frame contact sheet, chosen parameters, and reproducible render instructions. State any missing assets or unverified limitations. Distinguish photographed production from simulated appearance.
Framework contract: select the packages, runtime, timeline registration, validation commands, and renderer that actually belong to {{render_pipeline}}. Do not mix another framework's hooks, composition lifecycle, or renderer. Specialist modeling, photography, drawing, and scientific computation can produce inputs for the selected video framework without being replaced by it.
Palette contract: read palette before implementation. Use its suggested tokens only when task, brand, or reference colors are absent. Keep supplied exact colors, source artwork, existing semantic assignments, and style color-family and color-count constraints unchanged. Use chroma-js to validate and normalize equivalent color values, select readable existing foreground/background pairs, and interpolate only when palette.gradient is enabled. Do not recolor assets or add hues to improve contrast; change text placement, an existing backing color, or typography instead. Follow palette.agent_instruction and inspect actual composited frames.
Optional sketch rendering: when the brief calls for sketch-like marks, consult the Rough.js entry in tech.recommended_stack. Use package roughjs to generate seeded Canvas/SVG geometry, preserve the resolved palette, and follow its style_application and integration_guidance. Cache shapes; let the selected timeline animate transforms, masks, reveals or authored pose variants. Rough.js does not supply handwriting, authentic drawing media, a character rig or frame-by-frame poses. Keep precise text, measured geometry and approved source assets intact.
Shared movement quality: follow shared_motion_guidance and tech.motion_guidance. Design coherent trajectories, acceleration, transitions and settling with readable holds. Use time-based interpolation and authored easing when appropriate; preserve deliberate cuts, impacts, stepped exposure, whole-pixel placement and line-boil cadence. Do not automatically add springs, bounce, floating or extra in-between poses. Derive state from composition time; bake or deterministically replay any stateful smoothing, physics or camera damping. Verify direct, backward and out-of-order seeks plus the decoded sequence and loop seams. Keep the existing palette and style-specific motion direction intact.
Production ownership: follow production_policy. Choose the style_renderer and motion_engine from the style and motion requirements first, and state the selected tools and their responsibilities. Build the visuals and movement with those tools according to tech.implementation and visual_cues. Use {{render_pipeline}} only for scene assembly, seekable composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and export. Keep specialist rendering and motion logic in their own layers; do not substitute generic framework text, DOM transitions, or framework animation helpers merely because the pipeline is available. Native DOM or SVG is appropriate when it actually satisfies the style. Integrate deterministic time-driven layers or baked assets, and verify representative visuals and motion before assembling the full video.
Audio direction: follow audio_direction. Based on {{subject}}, {{audience_and_objective}}, the storyboard, visual_cues, and motion direction, suggest suitable background music, voiceover, sung vocals, sound effects, ambience, or silence. Honor {{audio_or_rhythm_requirements}} first. State the proposed choices and why they fit this topic and style; suggest mood, texture, energy, tempo where useful, voice language and delivery where useful, and scene-level audio changes. Do not impose a fixed soundtrack rule or include every layer. Source or create authorized assets, then use {{render_pipeline}} for assembly, synchronization, mixing, and export. Verify speech intelligibility, audio balance, absence of clipping, and picture synchronization in the final video.

motion_references.selection_policy: Optional candidates are screened for natural style compatibility. Before selection, inspect the actual scene illustration, assets, geometry and narrative beat. Keep only references whose defining action is supported by that scene. Choosing no reference is valid. Do not infer motion from a similar label; do not replace the existing style motion direction.

candidates.usage_guidance: Consider bounded pupil following with optional delayed brows, slight head tilt, and scheduled blinks. Require suitable facial layers or a rig, preserve expression and drawing cadence, and do not interpret this as viewer eye tracking.

Consider a progress-controlled handoff between outgoing and incoming chapters with synchronized copy and readable endpoints. Choose one compatible transition treatment and make both forward and backward state evaluation coherent.

Consider meaningful narrative steps with synchronized copy and visual states, plus optional within-step progress or sticky graphics. Use only scene-level motions that serve the story, and schedule the same states by time for video.

motion_references.agent_instruction: Read the actual illustration and complete pattern description, motion_sequence and video_adaptation. Identify which scene elements implement that action. Reject unsupported geometry, absent subjects, unintended depth, broken contact points or unrelated interactions. Select none when no candidate fits; use restrained style-native motion instead. Preserve authored transforms, fixed backgrounds and reading layers.

source_frame_review.sampling_limitation: One frame at each available second 01–08. No continuous motion, sub-second timing, audio or later scenes verified. Color families are visual observations; whole-frame measured dominant colors are not semantic background tokens.
source_frame_review.guidance: Choose scene-dependent backgrounds and readable coordinated colors. Separate material colors, source demonstration choices and surrounding UI/letterboxing. Existing swatches are examples, not permanent canvas restrictions. Keep explicit user-approved colors and medium-defining constraints. Only sampled seconds, not continuous motion or audio, were visually reviewed.

sources.style_evidence: The character keeps a stable body while its eye and expression shapes are replaced (dots, arcs, squares), and it rises, lands and turns. This suggests rigged parts with replaceable expressions rather than full redraws.
sources.palette_lesson: The fixed part of this example is a lighting-driven palette system laid over one unchanging landscape layout: the same mountains, lake, meadow, flowers and foliage are recolored for dusk (violet-to-peach), day (clear blue with an orange sun), cosmic night (indigo-violet nebula) and moonlit night (navy and slate). The character keeps a single warm terracotta local color throughout, so it is always the warmest and most saturated mass and stays the focal point against every sky. Glow effects (rings, HUD panels, fireflies, mushrooms) use pale cyan, white or yellow-green additive light and stay small. The specific sky hues, the planet and moon, and the terracotta mascot color are this author's choices for this subject, not style requirements. What carries over is one consistent local color for the hero, a sky/time-of-day gradient that sets the mood, and environment colors that shift together as a single lighting state.

sources.style_evidence: Characters keep the same drawn parts across pose changes (crouch, grip, boxing stance) and swap expressions. This looks like a puppet/rig workflow on a locked background rather than full redraws, but it cannot be confirmed from stills.
sources.palette_lesson: The sunny blue sky, warm-gray pavement, red bridge, dusty-blue skyline and gold crown are this author's choices for one daytime-city rivalry scene, not constraints of the style. What defines the style is a limited set of flat fills with no gradients except translucent light overlays, consistent dark outlines, clear figure-ground contrast (dark or saturated wardrobe against a light, low-detail backdrop), one glowing focal prop, and per-character color coding that can take over the frame in dramatic cutaways (blue vs peach strips on black). For new subjects, choose the environment hue from the setting and mood. Keep the set slightly lower in saturation and detail than the characters, and save the warmest, most saturated accent for the object of desire or conflict.

supporting_styles.role: Diagram drawing: contour connectors, arrows and paths the rigged presenter points to

suggestions.rationale: A rigged presenter gives explainer content warmth, while animated line art draws the mechanism the character explains without competing with the figure's fills.
suggestions.best_for: Character-hosted explainers, onboarding stories and educational shorts.
suggestions.video_application: The character anticipates and gestures, then the diagram draws itself in slate strokes from the hand's direction, with sage and terracotta reserved for highlighted paths; holds follow each completed structure.
suggestions.html_application: An SVG scene where each step button triggers a rig pose plus a DrawSVG-style path reveal; keyboard-focusable steps, prefers-reduced-motion shows the finished diagram with a static pose.
consistency_rules: Diagram strokes use the primary foreground token at one fixed width and cap style
Character pose lands before the related line starts drawing
Accents mark only the active path, never character fills and lines simultaneously
avoid: Diagram lines crossing the character's joints or face
Drawing connections continuously while the character idles

supporting_styles.role: Backgrounds: layered foreground/midground/background environment plates behind the rig

suggestions.rationale: Restrained parallax adds depth around a rigged character cheaply in PixiJS while the rig stays the only articulated element.
suggestions.best_for: Narrative scenes, walking or travel beats and storybook-like brand stories.
suggestions.video_application: Camera trucks slowly while background plates shift at small relative speeds; the rigged character walks on a midground ground line with consistent contact shadows.
suggestions.html_application: Scroll-linked parallax plates with a rigged character whose pose changes at section anchors; parallax is disabled under reduced motion and plates keep overscan to avoid exposed edges.
consistency_rules: Background plates use lower-contrast tints of the primary palette so the character holds luminance priority
Character occupies one depth layer and never drifts with plate speed
Plate edges extend beyond the crop at every camera position
avoid: Reversed depth speeds that make the character look pasted on

tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.

sources.style_evidence: Text carries the whole narrative: a typed prompt line with a caret, then a staged wordmark lockup built in reading order (eyebrow, title, rule, tagline), with clear holds and empty breathing frames between scenes.
sources.palette_lesson: The author's example colors are a warm near-black charcoal field, a rust-brown radial bloom, ivory type and a coral/terracotta accent. That is one brand-adjacent scene choice, not a fixed requirement. What defines the style is structural: one dark or quiet field with a single soft, low-contrast light source; one high-contrast neutral color for type; and one accent hue used only for thin functional marks (caret, divider rule, small eyebrow label). For new subjects, keep the three-role split and change the hues. Examples: a deep ink-navy field with a cool steel glow, bone-white type and amber accents for a night or tech topic; an oxblood field with blush type and gold-ochre rules for culture or wine; a forest-green field with a moss bloom, pale sage type and copper accents for nature; or a light mode with fog-gray paper, graphite type and a cobalt accent for a daytime or editorial piece. Keep the accent area tiny and check type contrast over the brightest part of the glow.

sources.style_evidence: The narrative is carried mostly by large extended-bold headlines ('BRO WAS / FAILING.', 'BRO WAS / LOCKED IN.'), a giant '68%' numeral, small monospace kickers, and two-tone emphasis on the payoff word. Each block is held for reading.
sources.palette_lesson: These are the author's example colours, not style rules. The transferable rules are these: background brightness and temperature encode the timeframe or mood and change at story cuts; one saturated alert colour is reserved for the verdict word and the 'you' row; other semantic colours appear only on functional UI (yellow for action/temptation, green for a healthy metric); and neutral off-white or near-black type does the setup. The scanline overlay is a constant across every palette. Adapting this to new subjects means choosing the alert colour and the scene fields from the topic, not reusing crimson on black or khaki.

audio_direction.prompt: Based on the topic, audience, objective, narrative, and the visual and motion characteristics of Kinetic Typography, suggest an appropriate audio direction. Consider background music, voiceover, sung vocals, sound effects, ambience, or intentional silence. Explain which choices support this particular video; do not assign a fixed genre, tempo, instrument, voice, or mandatory audio layer to the style.
suggestion_dimensions: Whether background music is useful, and its suggested mood, texture, energy, tempo range, and progression.
Whether voiceover helps explain the topic, and its suggested language, tone, pace, and placement.
Whether sung vocals support the topic or distract from narration and essential text.
Whether sound effects, ambience, or silence clarify key actions, transitions, and reading holds.
How audio changes across scenes, supports motion cadence, and leaves space for speech and comprehension.
audio_direction.selection_guidance: Treat these as task-specific suggestions, not requirements to include every audio layer. Honor explicit user audio choices and supplied assets. audio_direction.integration_guidance: Select or create authorized audio assets separately from visual construction and motion design. Use render_pipeline to assemble, synchronize, mix, and export audio with picture. Keep speech intelligible, avoid clipping and competing vocals, and inspect the delivered audio and picture together.

suggested_combinations.selection_guidance: Kinetic Typography stands alone for quotes, manifestos and copy-led spots. Combine it when timing must follow music or when dense copy needs a rigid grid, letting the support govern timing or layout while words stay the narrative.

supporting_styles.role: Timing: beat and section map that schedules word entrances and holds

suggestions.best_for: Lyric videos, rhythmic promos and spoken-word pieces with a supplied track.
suggestions.video_application: Key words land on downbeats, supporting words fill offbeats, and choruses raise density; the red accent marks only stressed words.
suggestions.html_application: Audio-synced HTML/CSS text timeline seeking from audio currentTime; captions always present, and a no-audio mode advances on keyboard input.

avoid: Diagonal free-floating motion breaking the grid

styles.visual_cues: Build a continuous visual system from a few shapes and limited colors with deliberate proportions and centers of gravity. Use repetition, division, merging, rotation, and varied timing; let each state lead into the next. Avoid unrelated particles or light effects that weaken the structural motif.
styles.note: The source directly names or describes this visual direction.

tech.implementation: Use reusable shape groups and shared coordinates for repetition and assembly. Use an existing path-interpolation library for complex morphing.
tech.render_pipeline:
Composition and export only: follow production_policy; integrate output from tech.style_renderer and tech.motion_engine.
Primary: HyperFrames. Author HTML/CSS/SVG compositions with data-composition-id, data-width, data-height, and data-duration. Time class="clip" elements with data-start and data-duration. Register one paused, seekable GSAP timeline per composition in window.__timelines[compositionId]; let the framework control media time. Run npx hyperframes check, inspect key moments with npx hyperframes snapshot --at <seconds>, and render with npx hyperframes render --quality delivery --output <video.mp4> under the task's authorization. Load local fonts and assets first, seed randomness, and drive Canvas/WebGL from shared time rather than wall clocks or independent loops.
Fallback: Remotion. Use this route only when HyperFrames is unavailable or cannot meet a required constraint, and document the checked limitation. Build React/Remotion compositions driven by useCurrentFrame and useVideoConfig, preload assets, seed randomness, and render through the Remotion CLI or @remotion/renderer in Node.js. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
Delivery checks: inspect decoded opening, action, transition, and closing frames and watch the full video. Verify dimensions, duration, frame rate, audio synchronization, and loop continuity; fix issues and rerender.
tech.usage_note: These are suggested implementation routes, not claims about the source video's actual toolchain or locally installed tools. Tool combinations are selected as needed. Native Canvas and SVG do not require a 3D engine. Prepare assets and cache stateful simulations first; a simulated appearance is not evidence of physical production or validated physics. Reference numbers, scenes, and aspect ratios are optional examples.

framework_selection.fallback_condition: Use Remotion only when HyperFrames is unavailable in the current environment or a verified limitation prevents a required capability or output. Record the specific reason. An existing React project alone is not a fallback reason.
framework_selection.scope: Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export. HyperFrames is the first choice; Remotion is the conditional fallback. Neither is the default visual construction or motion design method.

tech.library_selection: Choose libraries by role and scene requirements; the available options are not a required bundle. Prefer existing suitable dependencies. Use one owner for each animated property. Preserve HyperFrames as the primary video framework and Remotion as the conditional fallback. For video, drive all state from seekable composition time; live hover, scroll, and pointer behavior belongs only to interactive delivery. Select visual and motion technologies from the style, action, assets, and required fidelity before choosing the composition and export pipeline. Pipeline availability must not determine or simplify the visual style or motion technique. Owns scene assembly, composition timing, media and audio synchronization, validation, and final export.
